[1] rewrite

```
- **Why the step-size test allows a 0.5% gap between runs.** No record says
  how 0.5% was chosen. It dates from an earlier, approximate method, whose runs
  differed by about 0.04% in the alveolar concentration and by more in mixed
  venous. The test also requires each gap to stay below 1e-14 as a fraction.
  Any gap that breaks 0.5% is at least 1e-8, the absolute tolerance, so it
  breaks 1e-14 too. Today the 0.5% limit therefore never changes the test's
  result.
```

[2] rewrite

```
- **How to change the step-size test's limits.** A fork with an approximate
  method fails the 1e-14 limit even when its arithmetic is correct. For example,
  a first-order method shows gaps near 1.4e-11. Relax 1e-14, and 0.5% becomes
  the working check. Set it above the method's own gaps at the test's steps and
  below a difference a learner could see. The constants are in
  `tests/reference/test_sevo_patient.py`.
```

[3] rewrite

```
**The release check on step length, and why it allows a 0.5% difference.** The
model advances in fixed steps of 0.1 s. A shorter step should give almost the
same result. Before each release, a test reruns the first minute of the default
sevoflurane induction with steps of 0.1 s, 0.05 s and 0.025 s. Each run's
alveolar, vessel-rich and mixed-venous concentrations must be within 0.5% of the
run with the next shorter step. A compartment that holds almost no agent also
passes if its two values differ by less than 0.000001 vol%, because there a tiny
difference is a large percentage. The 0.5% was set for the simulator's earlier
calculation method, at about ten times the 0.04% alveolar difference that method
showed. On 2026-10-03, the current method's runs agreed to better than one part
in a trillion, so the much tighter limits in the paragraphs above are the ones
that would catch a real error.
```

[4] rewrite

```
The 5e-3 relative tolerance was chosen when the simulator used an earlier
calculation method, the operator split. That method showed a relative gap of
4e-4 in the alveolar fraction between steps of 0.1 s and 0.025 s, and 5e-3 is
about ten times that gap. The tolerance is kept as a coarse check, because the
current method, the exact step, gave relative gaps of about 1.4e-13 when the
same comparison was run on 2026-10-03. For a fraction so close to zero that a
relative gap means little, the 1e-8 absolute tolerance lets a negligible
difference pass.
```

[5] rewrite

```
**The release check on step length.** The simulator moves the model forward in
fixed time steps, normally 0.1 s long. A shorter step should give almost the
same result. If it does not, the step is too long. Before each release, a test
runs the first minute of the default sevoflurane induction three times, with
steps of 0.1 s, 0.05 s and 0.025 s. In each run, the alveolar, vessel-rich and
mixed-venous concentrations must be within 0.5% of the run with the next
shorter step. For a compartment that still holds almost no agent, a tiny
difference can be a large percentage, so a percentage means little. Two values
for such a compartment also pass if they differ by less than 0.000001 vol%, one
part in a hundred million of the gas. On 2026-10-03, with the current
calculation method, the three runs agreed to better than one part in a trillion,
so this check is now only a coarse safety net. The much tighter limit in the
paragraphs above is the one that would catch a real error.

**Why the release check allows a 0.5% difference.** The 0.5% margin was set for
the simulator's earlier calculation method. With that method, the alveolar
concentrations of the 0.1 s and 0.025 s runs differed by about 0.04%, so the
margin allowed about ten times that difference. The check compares each run only
with the next shorter step. Under the earlier method, a direct comparison of the
0.1 s run with the 0.025 s run would have failed, because their mixed-venous
concentrations differed by 0.55%. At one minute, those concentrations have
barely begun to rise.
```

[6] rewrite

```
**The maximum dial settings for the three agents come from two classes of vaporizer.** The
sevoflurane and isoflurane maxima are those of variable-bypass dials. Desflurane's is the top of
the range of the Tec 6, a heated gas–vapour blender. The model fixes ambient pressure at 760 mmHg
(§ "Assumptions"). At that pressure, the same dial setting on either class gives the same partial
pressure, so the model does not need to know which class a maximum came from. The classes would
differ only at reduced ambient pressure, which is not modelled (§ "Known limitations").
```
